{"id": "33:72/q18", "question": "Why are mountains named separately after earth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:72/q18/p1", "position": "They are a particular singled out after the general earth to emphasize their distinction and the trust's great weight.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the middle prayer, Gabriel, and dates and pomegranates (2:238, 2:98, 55:68); he calls mountains the greatest earthly creations and their mention fitting for a weighty burden."}, {"id": "33:72/q18/p2", "position": "Their special place in creation includes stabilizing earth and occurring throughout the celestial bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī invokes the mountains as earth's anchors in 31:10 and says mountains also occur throughout the celestial bodies."}, {"id": "33:72/q18/p3", "position": "Their firmness highlights the still greater steadfastness of the trust, which steadies believers on the Bridge.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares mountains stabilizing earth (31:10) with believers steadied by God's word (14:27), concluding that the trust outlasts mountains and is firmer than they are."}]}
{"id": "35:37/q01", "question": "Who are the people crying in the Fire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q01/p1", "position": "The disbelievers condemned to Hell, continuing the people of 35:36.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the pronoun to the disbelievers of 35:36 and coordinates this clause with their having the Fire, rather than making it circumstantial; Study Quran likewise describes disbelievers facing the judgment they denied."}]}
{"id": "35:37/q02", "question": "What does يَصْطَرِخُونَ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q02/p1", "position": "They cry loudly and intensely for help or rescue in Hell.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn Jurayj gloss it as seeking help. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bayḍāwī connect the plea to ṣarākh, a loud cry; al-Thaʿlabī says ṣārikh can name either supplicant or helper, while al-Qurṭubī distinguishes ṣārikh from muṣrikh and cites a poem about a frightened caller and hoofbeats. Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nasafī, al-Bursawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the verb's intensity and the sufferers' helplessness. Al-Bursawī also says it is used for seeking intercession. Their following plea explains the cry, according to al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī. Al-Zarkashī says the fuller form yaṣṭarikhūn intensifies the cries beyond yataṣārakhūn. Al-Suyūṭī likewise contrasts it with ordinary yaṣrukhūn. Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the lengthened endings of 33:66–67, where people stretch their cries in Hell, with the ordinary form in 33:4."}]}
{"id": "35:37/q03", "question": "How is the form يَصْطَرِخُونَ derived?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q03/p1", "position": "It is an intensive iftiʿāl form from ṣarākh or ṣurākh, with the form's tāʾ changed to ṭāʾ near emphatic ṣād.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya explain the nearby articulation and emphatic matching; al-Wāḥidī cites iṣṭarakha and taṣārakhū. Al-Bursawī describes the inserted emphatic letter as strengthening the cry. Al-Samīn's note describes the consonant change differently, saying tāʾ changes to ṣād before ṭāʾ. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the intensive form with yaṣrukhūn. Al-Zarkashī says added morphological form brings added meaning and uses yaṣṭarikhūn versus yataṣārakhūn as an example; he also transmits al-Khalīl's sound-shape comparison of the extended cricket call and segmented hawk cry. Al-Suyūṭī states the broader principle that diction matches the force of its meaning and calls yaṣṭarikhūn stronger than yaṣrukhūn."}]}

{"id": "35:37/q10", "question": "What is the force of the question أَوَلَمْ نُعَمِّرْكُم?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q10/p1", "position": "It answers and rebukes their plea by confirming that God gave them ample time to reflect, repent, and heed warning.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda calls it rhetorical confirmation, not information-seeking; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it censure. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr stress that the time allowed any willing person to benefit. Al-Suyūṭī calls this question reproach for failure to reflect during an adequate lifespan: its formal negation intends affirmation, unlike denial that nullifies a proposition; he also calls this use reprimand and distinguishes acknowledgment of a settled fact. Ibn Jinnī and Sībawayh, as transmitted through Abū Ḥayyān, reserve acknowledgment questioning for hamza rather than hal. {"id": "35:37/q17", "question": "Who or what is ٱلنَّذِيرُ?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning is delivered by a messenger or scripture, or embodied in life signs and reason; proponents of the Messenger cite other verses and binding scriptural proof, while gray-hair proponents cite usage, poetry and signs of death.", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q17/p1", "position": "Muhammad, God's messenger, came as the warner.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Zayd cite 53:56; al-Wāḥidī cites 33:45 and 48:8; Ibn Jarīr as reported by Ibn Kathīr cites 43:77–78, 17:15 and 67:8–9. {"id": "35:37/q40", "question": "What Arabic ending patterns provide grammatical parallels for نَعْمَلْ and نَّصِيرٍ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q40/p1", "position": "Poetic rhyme may alter final vowels or long letters, while hesitant ordinary speech may lengthen an ending or add kasra before resuming.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says poets may add a rhyme yāʾ after hāʾ, retain an alif as al-Khalīl recites, drop a wāw, or vocalize a still or jussive rhyme ending for meter, especially with kasra in genitive rhyme; he cites lines of Imruʾ al-Qays and Ṭarafa. In ordinary hesitation he reports lengthening after qāla and yaqūlu and kasra after qad or with tanwin, as in sayf-ni, to keep the utterance open. Sībawayh says sung rhyme prolongs endings with alif, yāʾ or wāw, with or without tanwīn, matching the preceding vowel because poetry is made for singing; he illustrates different inflections with lines of Imruʾ al-Qays (manzilī), Yazīd ibn al-Thaʿthariyya (maṣraʿā), al-Aʿshā (lāʾimū) and Jarīr (al-ʿitābā, al-khiyāmū, al-ayyāmā). He reports that Hijaz reciters retain these endings even without melody to mark verse, many Tamīmīs replace the length letter with nūn, as in al-ʿAjjāj's al-dharfan and annahajan, and a third practice drops prolongation, as in Jarīr's al-ʿitāb and al-Akhṭal's faʿal. When the preceding consonant is the rhyme, final yāʾ and wāw may be treated like appended length letters and even a weak radical may be omitted; al-Khalīl distinguishes yāʾ and wāw retained as the rhyme letter itself in yaqḍī and yaghzū, as qāf is in his cited line. Sībawayh says alif remains in yakhshā and yarḍā as in ordinary speech, unlike deletable yāʾ; al-Khalīl cites poetry retaining the alif of ṭayrā like taqaḍḍā and deleting the wāw of taqaddamū. Sībawayh says many of Qays and Asad even omit pronominal yāʾ and wāw, less often because they convey noun meaning; he cites omitted plural endings in ṣanaʿ, qanaʿ, jamaʿ and Ibn Muqbil's awjaf, and feminine endings in ʿAntara's takallam and al-Khazzāz ibn Lawdhān's idhhab, while the hāʾ in shattā ṭarāʾiquhu is retained because it is not a weak or length letter. He explains that a still or jussive rhyme ending can be moved and lengthened as poetic license, requiring kasra in genitive rhyme lest nominative or accusative rhyme be iqwāʾ; lines of Imruʾ al-Qays and Ṭarafa and Abū al-Najm's rajaz ending in ḥulī and maskanah illustrate this. In ordinary hesitation, Sībawayh adds examples of lengthening a final vowel (qālā, yaqūlū, al-ʿām) and using kasra on a final consonant (qadī, alī, sayfnī) to keep speech open while recollecting."}]}

Kuranyolu names faith, piety and excellence as conditions of a good Muslim life."}, {"id": "39:10/q05/p3", "position": "Use God as protection from everything besides Him and remove the veil of attachment.", "reasons": "Bursawī describes escape from separation and joy in divine beauty; al-Baqlī makes taqwā stripping the self of attachment until it stands unveiled."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q06", "question": "Does the command to believers imply grave sin removes faith?", "turns_on": "Whether grave sin cancels faith and its reward or faith remains despite sin.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q06/p1", "position": "No: faith remains even when a believer has not fulfilled taqwā.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues that commanding believers to add God-consciousness presupposes faith with sin; exhortation is stronger if they remain believers when they fall short."}, {"id": "39:10/q06/p2", "position": "Avoidance of major sins preserves faith's reward; grave sin cancels it.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī says the command protects faith and its recompense from nullification. Al-Rāzī rejects the implication."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q07", "question": "What is the iʿrāb of ٱتَّقُوا۟?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q07/p1", "position": "Its tāʾ replaces an original wāw.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives the morphological observation, repeated by al-Qurṭubī."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q08", "question": "What does doing good, أَحْسَنُوا۟, entail?", "turns_on": "Whether excellence is described by outward acts, the Prophetic definition of worship, or an inward realization.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q08/p1", "position": "It includes faithful obedience, righteous conduct, and kindness to others.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī calls the doers believers acting well; al-Qushayrī says excellence is doing all one can; al-Wāḥidī specifies monotheists who obey; al-Jishumī includes generosity and inviting others to religion; al-Ṭabrisī says virtuous acts and kindness. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates them to the God-fearing in 39:9 and says the relative phrase embraces all with the quality. Bursawī stresses sincerity and the testimony of faith; a bad deed cannot earn good recompense."}, {"id": "39:10/q08/p2", "position": "Iḥsān is worshipping God as though seeing Him, aware that He sees the worshipper.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the Prophetic definition; Bursawī and Ālūsī invoke the Gabriel report, with Bursawī adding that witnessing brings full sincerity and guards against ostentation and shirk. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates this to the devout of 39:9."}, {"id": "39:10/q08/p3", "position": "Inward excellence is seeking God alone and witnessing His beauty.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī speaks of effacing attributes and taking on divine attributes; Najm al-Dīn says sincere seekers ask no good from others and find God; al-Khujandī's poem makes seeking the key to the treasure; al-Baqlī describes unveiling in heart and spirit. Ālūsī gives exclusive seeking."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q09", "question": "What good is promised to those who do good?", "turns_on": "Whether “in this world” locates good deeds or the reward, and whether the promise is confined to one realm.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q09/p1", "position": "Paradise is the good reward for goodness done in this world.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Jishumī, al-Rāzī and many later sources locate reward in the Hereafter. Al-Rāzī argues the indefinite good is majestic and lasting, that unbelievers share health, and that the restrictive wording excludes shared worldly benefits (43:33); he cites the saying that worldly life is a believer's prison and unbeliever's garden. Al-Qushayrī makes the same worldly-benefits objection in al-Qurṭubī. Al-Ālūsī's opening exposition treats the indefinite as magnification; Bursevi adds vision of God."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p2", "position": "Worldly health, safety, sufficiency, and well-being are the good.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī is cited by al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī and others. Al-Rāzī reports a saying naming security, health and sufficiency as inexhaustible blessings. Abū Ḥayyān adds success and divine protection; al-Ṭabrisī adds thanks and reputation. Al-Ālūsī describes this as an immediate small share, but objects that unbelievers too receive health, citing 41:50; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the proposed attachment to ḥasana."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p3", "position": "Goodness includes reward in this world and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers worldly reward besides final recompense; al-Qurṭubī replies that grateful believers receive both; Ibn Kathīr states both. Al-Biqāʿī prefers breadth across both realms. Ālūsī later prefers both, with inward and outward action; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists peace of mind, sound soul and freedom from dependence here, lasting delight there. Kuranyolu prefers the unrestricted promise; Study Quran likewise allows health and peace here and good beyond."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p4", "position": "The worldly good is praise, good reputation, kind words, or God's guardianship.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās includes God's friendship, praise and good names; al-Māwardī proposes praise with next-life recompense. Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī cite praise and gratitude; al-Qurṭubī reports a good reputation; al-Ālūsī says God's guardianship is distinctive to believers."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p5", "position": "The worldly good is victory, spoils, divine support, or relief from enemies.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh says victory and spoils; Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports al-Suddī's victory and support gloss, though he prefers the Hereafter. ʿAṭāʾ, reported by Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī, ties relief from enemies to emigrating to Medina; al-Qurṭubī includes victory and booty."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p6", "position": "Inwardly the good is finding God, seeing His enduring Face, and divine unveiling.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls divine vision the good of those witnessing; Najm al-Dīn and Ālūsī describe finding God. Al-Baqlī distinguishes worldly inspirations from immersion in eternity and abiding in the attributes hereafter."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p7", "position": "The worldly good is obedience granted in this life, with Paradise in the next.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan's distinction is transmitted by al-Māwardī; al-Qurṭubī likewise distinguishes first good as obedience from second as Paradise."}, {"id": "39:10/q09/p8", "position": "It is whatever good God gives in worldly life.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām states the broad gloss; al-Jishumī also reports Muqātil's generic “goodness.” Ibn ʿĀshūr says the promise of worldly goodness explains the address to the pious and prepares the assurance of broad safe lands; it may also ground the command to fear God."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q10", "question": "How does فِى هَٰذِهِ ٱلدُّنْيَا attach syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the prepositional phrase modifies the act, the reward, or deliberately allows both.", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q10/p1", "position": "It modifies أَحْسَنُوا۟, placing the doing of good in this world.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and others report this; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī favor it with Paradise as reward. Al-Samīn says an omitted qualifier magnifies ḥasana. Bursawī parses ḥasana as subject and li-lladhīna as predicate. Ibn ʿĀshūr says this also urges action before opportunity passes; Ālūsī's primary exposition agrees."}, {"id": "39:10/q10/p2", "position": "It locates or describes حَسَنَةٌۭ, making worldly good the direct promise.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās report this parse; al-Zamakhsharī says a preceding phrase can specify location despite not being a following adjective. Al-Samīn makes it a fronted adjective with an omitted circumstantial element. Al-Biqāʿī calls a new subject-predicate worldly clause too narrow; Ālūsī records al-Suddī and al-Zamakhsharī, yet criticizes a circumstantial modifier of an indefinite subject and al-Akhfash's weak analysis. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the attachment."}, {"id": "39:10/q10/p3", "position": "Its central placement permits both worldly and afterlife senses.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī prefers a broad reading. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the placement is deliberate and allows multiple meanings; the indefinite reward can magnify either otherworldly essence or worldly quality."}]}
{"id": "39:10/q11", "question": "What does the word حَسَنَةٌۭ contribute to the promise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:10/q11/p1", "position": "Its indefiniteness magnifies the promised good.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī's view, via al-Samīn, supplies an omitted “great”; Ālūsī says the indefinite magnifies Paradise. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it can magnify afterlife reward intrinsically or worldly good qualitatively, with 2:201 as a comparison."}, {"id": "39:10/q11/p2", "position": "It stands for a good condition, with a noun elided.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the transfer of adjective to noun in 2:201 and the inverse expression in 42:40."}, {"id": "39:10/q11/p3", "position": "The fronted لِلَّذِينَ draws attention to the recipients of divine kindness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the word order to an invitation to become God-fearing doers of good."}]}
